candidates.title: Orbital Matter, EnduroSat Announce an In-Space Manufacturing Mission in 2028
candidates.raw_excerpt: Following off the success of its latest demo, in-space manufacturing startup Orbital Matter announced today that it would partner with EnduroSat for another mission in 2028, this time to deploy a 5 kW solar array with the help of Orbital Matter’s 3D printing capabilities. The demo aims to validate a new method to create large structures in orbit. Instead of folding bulky solar arrays into tight configurations to fit into launch vehicles, the companies plan to 3D print support structures in space to facilitate large solar-array deployments. “Basically, [folding] means that you need to design and develop all the space systems—all the spacecraft—mostly for the launch, and not for operations in orbit,” CEO Jakub Stojek told Payload.  Copy and paste: The announcement comes shortly after Orbital Matter released results of its second demonstration mission, called Replicator 2, which proved the company’s ability to print structures in the vacuum of space for the first time.  Replicator 2, launched on SpaceX’s Transporter-17 rideshare in July, using an EnduroSat bus. It carried four Orbital Matter printers, each equipped with liquid material which could be printed onto a spinning cylinder, and hardened using a UV light. As it prints, the hardened beam pushes out and holds a silicon solar blanket. Replicator 2 attempted its first print job in August, where it ultimately failed to create a fully viable structure, as there were gaps between layers of printed material. candidates.title: On this day in space! Nov. 3, 1957: Laika the dog launches with Sputnik 2
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Nov. 3, 1957, a Soviet space dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth. Laika was a 3-year-old stray husky-spitz mix from the streets of Moscow, and she was recruited by the Soviet space program for her small size and calm temperament. Unfortunately for Laika, this mission was a one-way trip . The Soviets didn't design a way to bring her back down to Earth. With only 7 days worth of oxygen and a little bit of food on board, Laika launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan with a Russian Sputnik rocket. This was the same kind of rocket used to launch the first Sputnik satellite. Laika was alive when she reached orbit, but she died shortly afterward because the spacecraft's heat shield had broken off. Laika overheated before she had the chance to die of starvation of oxygen deprivation. Laika, the first Soviet space dog to enter Earth orbit, is seen in a training capsule prior to her launch. (Image credit: Roscosmos) Why it mattered Laika has remained one of space history's most beloved and tragic figures. People around the world have dogs as pets who they love as members of their own families. And even nearly 70 years after this flight, it is so heartbreaking to think of Laika on that frightening journey from which she never returned. Laika was one of many different animals that were used in early spaceflight testing. Both the U.S. and Russia launched a number of primates on flights testing early flight technology. Sadly, like Laika, many of these brave creatures did not make it back. Unbelievably, though, some did survive the journey. For example, the chimpanzee named Ham and nicknamed the "astrochimp" survived a 1961 test flight to space. Though, the team behind that flight was so unsure of how it would go that Ham didn't get his name until after it was found that he'd survived his return. Want more space history? candidates.raw_excerpt: Betelguese, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, has been putting on quite a show lately — but not in the way you might expect. The famous red supergiant in the constellation Orion has been growing noticeably fainter in recent months. Of the 21 brightest stars in the night sky, Betelgeuse is perhaps the most enigmatic. Its changing brightness poses a puzzle: how do the star's pulsations, dust eruptions, and a possible companion contribute to its fading? A giant star with a puzzling name Even the translation of Betelgeuse's name is contentious. For a long time, it was thought to be a corruption of three Arabic words, usually translated as "The Armpit of the Giant." However, other experts in star nomenclature now dispute that interpretation, proposing instead "The Hand of al-Jauzā," with al-Jauzā referring to Orion. Although classified as a red supergiant, Betelgeuse usually appears more orange than red— golden orange or deep topaz. It is one of the most famous stars in its class. Henry M. Neely (1877-1963), for many years a popular lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium , described its restless behavior in his book A Primer for Stargazers : "(Betelgeuse) expands and contracts spasmodically, like an old man with his strength almost entirely spent, panting in the asthmatic decrepitude of old age." The rhythms of a changing star Betelgeuse naturally expands and contracts like a beating heart. As an aging red supergiant, it has a regular pulsation cycle of roughly 430 days: when it expands, its outer layers cool and it dims; when it contracts, they heat up and it brightens. Among first-magnitude stars — the brightest category of stars in the night sky — it is the only marked variable. Its scale is equally remarkable: located 650 light-years away, Betelgeuse is among the largest and most luminous stars of its class, with a luminosity of about 14,000 suns at maximum and 7,600 suns at minimum. candidates.title: ChatGPT Is Giving Voters Ludicrous Misinformation Right as the Midterms Hit
candidates.raw_excerpt: As crucial elections loom in the United States, AI chatbots are dumping political misinformation onto the populace with astonishing confidence. There’s evidence that the problem is widespread. According to recent reporting by the Washington Post , top AI chatbots are giving horribly flawed information to users asking for voting guides on the midterms. For example, when WaPo tasked ChatGPT with creating a voter guide for all the races and candidates relevant to a resident of Missouri, the chatbot added a Senate seat that isn’t even up for re-election. A similar test for a resident in Wyoming claimed that local politicians running in municipal elections were running for federal seats. In all, WaPo took a look at 3,000 AI-generated voting guides, which frequently shared false voting information that usually traced back to other AI-generated websites . In other words, the AI chatbots are eating their own slop and passing it off as authoritative election information. Overall, the paper found chatbots failed to find which congressional district an exact address was located in a whopping 48 percent of the time, while those that did got it wrong 22 percent of the time. Luckily, the share of users actually querying the chatbots seems to be relatively low. According to a late-October survey by the Pew Research Center, just eight percent of US voters say they’ve used an AI chatbot like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini to look up information relevant to the ballot-box. While the ideal number would be zero voters in any nation receiving AI-generated election misinformation, it seems in 2026, we’ll have to take what we can get. "We designed [JWST] to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time," Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America said in a statement .
